reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: The hallmark is an audible or palpable snap or clunk felt during hip movement
The external type is caused by the iliotibial band or gluteus maximus tendon flicking over the greater trochanter, giving lateral symptoms
The internal type is caused by the iliopsoas tendon shifting over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head, giving anterior or groin symptoms
The intra-articular type is caused by a labral tear, loose body or chondral lesion
It most often affects young active people such as dancers and athletes and is frequently painless, though it can become symptomatic
The external snap can often be reproduced and even seen by the patient, whereas the internal snap is elicited by extending the hip from a flexed, abducted, externally rotated position
Dynamic ultrasound is particularly useful to demonstrate the offending tendon snapping in real time

Generic management includes activity modification, stretching and physiotherapy, corticosteroid injection into the bursa or iliopsoas sheath, and surgical lengthening, release or arthroscopy for refractory or intra-articular causes
reference.pathophysiology: Snapping hip syndrome describes a snapping sensation produced when a tendon or band catches on a bony prominence, or when an intra-articular lesion mechanically catches. In the external type the iliotibial band or gluteus maximus tendon flicks across the greater trochanter, while in the internal type the iliopsoas tendon abruptly shifts over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head as the hip extends from a flexed position. The intra-articular type stems from labral tears or loose bodies. Repetitive movement of the offending structure commonly leads to a secondary tendinopathy or bursitis that generates pain.
additionalDifferentials: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome or trochanteric bursitis
Intra-articular loose body or chondral lesion
additionalInvestigations: Dynamic ultrasound as a first-line study to demonstrate the snapping tendon
Clinical reproduction manoeuvres for the external and internal types
Plain radiographs to assess bony morphology, impingement and osteoarthritis
MRI or MR arthrography to evaluate the labrum and intra-articular structures
A diagnostic injection into the iliopsoas sheath or bursa to confirm the pain source
redFlags: Intra-articular mechanical symptoms such as locking suggesting a loose body or labral tear
Night pain or systemic features raising concern for tumour or infection
Progressive activity-related pain suggesting a femoral neck stress fracture
reference.prognosis: Most patients respond to conservative measures, and surgery reserved for refractory cases generally gives good results, though intra-articular causes require specific treatment.
pitfalls: Missing intra-articular pathology by labelling all snapping as a benign tendon cause
Overtreating asymptomatic snapping that needs only reassurance
Causing iatrogenic weakness through excessive tendon lengthening
Failing to use dynamic imaging to confirm the mechanism
management: First-line conservative management with activity modification, targeted physiotherapy stretching and strengthening of the iliotibial band or iliopsoas, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Corticosteroid injection into the trochanteric bursa or iliopsoas sheath for painful tendinopathy or bursitis, which can also be diagnostic.
Surgical release or lengthening of the iliotibial band in the external type or the iliopsoas tendon in the internal type, reserved for refractory symptomatic cases.
Hip arthroscopy to address an intra-articular cause such as a labral tear, loose body or chondral lesion.
Reassure patients with painless snapping, for whom no intervention beyond load management is needed.
Refer to orthopaedics or hip-preservation surgery for symptoms resistant to conservative care.
